text: Given an array of integers, find two numbers that add up to a specific target and return their indices.
ideal_answer_points: Recognizes the brute-force O(n^2) nested-loop approach first, then improves on it
Uses a hash map to store seen values and their indices, checking for the complement in O(1) per element
Achieves O(n) time, O(n) space with a single pass
Clarifies whether duplicate values or multiple valid pairs need special handling
Discusses the tradeoff versus sorting + two pointers (O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, but loses original indices)

text: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
ideal_answer_points: Identifies this as a sliding window problem, not brute force over all substrings
Maintains a window with a hash set or hash map of characters currently in the window
Expands the right pointer and shrinks the left pointer when a duplicate is found
Achieves O(n) time by ensuring each character is visited a bounded number of times
Correctly handles edge cases: empty string, all-unique string, all-same-character string

text: Reverse a singly linked list, both iteratively and recursively.
ideal_answer_points: Iterative approach: maintains prev, current, and next pointers, reversing links one node at a time
Correctly re-points current.next to prev before advancing all three pointers
Recursive approach: recurses to the end of the list, then reverses links on the way back up the call stack
States time complexity O(n) for both, space complexity O(1) iterative vs O(n) recursive due to call stack
Can explain the tradeoff: recursive is more elegant but risks stack overflow on very long lists

text: Given a linked list, determine if it contains a cycle, and if so, find the node where the cycle begins.
ideal_answer_points: Uses Floyd's Tortoise and Hare technique: two pointers moving at different speeds
Explains why the pointers must meet inside the cycle if one exists
For finding the cycle's start: after detecting a meeting point, resets one pointer to the head and advances both at the same speed until they meet again
States O(n) time, O(1) space, and can contrast with the O(n) space HashSet alternative
Handles edge cases: empty list, single node, no cycle

text: Given a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).
ideal_answer_points: Recognizes that checking only immediate parent-child relationships is insufficient
Uses a recursive approach that tracks a valid (min, max) range for each node as it descends
Alternative: in-order traversal should produce a strictly increasing sequence for a valid BST
Correctly handles duplicate values and defines whether they're allowed
States O(n) time, O(h) space where h is tree height (call stack)

text: Given a 2D grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands.
ideal_answer_points: Recognizes this as a connected-components problem on an implicit graph
Uses DFS or BFS from each unvisited land cell, marking connected land cells as visited
Correctly handles 4-directional (or specifies 8-directional) adjacency
Avoids revisiting cells, either via a visited set or by mutating the grid in place
States O(rows * cols) time and space complexity

text: Given an array of integers, find the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
ideal_answer_points: Starts from the O(n^2) DP formulation: dp[i] = longest subsequence ending at index i
Correctly defines the recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1) for all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]
Can improve to O(n log n) using patience sorting with binary search over a 'tails' array
Explains why the O(n log n) tails array doesn't directly represent the actual subsequence, only its length
Handles edge cases: empty array, strictly decreasing array, all-equal elements

text: Implement a queue using two stacks.
ideal_answer_points: Uses one stack for enqueue operations, one for dequeue operations
On dequeue, if the 'dequeue stack' is empty, pops everything from the 'enqueue stack' and pushes it onto the 'dequeue stack' to reverse order
Explains amortized O(1) time per operation, even though a single dequeue can be O(n) in the worst case
Correctly handles the empty-queue edge case
Can discuss the reverse problem (stack using two queues) as a related follow-up

text: Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together.
ideal_answer_points: Identifies that anagrams share a canonical form when sorted or when represented as a character-count signature
Uses a hash map keyed by that canonical form, appending matching strings to the same bucket
Discusses the tradeoff: sorting each string (O(k log k) per string) vs. a character-count key (O(k) per string)
States overall time complexity in terms of n strings of average length k
Handles edge cases: empty strings, single-character strings

text: Given a set of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set).
ideal_answer_points: Recognizes there are 2^n subsets and frames the approach around that
Uses backtracking: at each element, recursively explores both including and excluding it
Alternative: iterative bit-manipulation approach, treating each subset as a binary mask over n elements
Correctly avoids duplicate subsets when the input may contain duplicate values (sorts first, skips repeated choices at the same recursion depth)
States O(2^n) time and space, since all subsets must be generated and stored

text: Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly.
ideal_answer_points: Clarifies requirements: expected read/write ratio, custom aliases, expiration, analytics needs
Proposes a short-code generation strategy (base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing ID, or a hash with collision handling) and explains the tradeoff chosen
Designs the core schema: short_code, long_url, created_at, expiry, owner
Addresses read-heavy traffic with caching (e.g., Redis) in front of the database for hot redirects
Discusses horizontal scaling of the redirect service and database sharding/replication as traffic grows

text: Design a rate limiter that can be applied to an API to prevent abuse.
ideal_answer_points: Compares algorithm choices: fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter, token bucket — and picks one with justification
Explains why token bucket is often preferred for allowing controlled bursts while enforcing an average rate
Discusses where state lives: in-memory per-instance (fast but inconsistent across a fleet) vs. centralized store like Redis (consistent but adds latency/dependency)
Addresses what happens when the limit is exceeded (429 response, retry-after header)
Considers rate-limiting granularity: per-user, per-IP, per-API-key, and how that changes the design

text: Design a real-time one-on-one and group messaging system like WhatsApp.
ideal_answer_points: Chooses a persistent connection strategy (WebSockets or long polling) for real-time delivery and justifies it
Designs message storage and ordering, including how to handle out-of-order delivery across devices
Addresses delivery guarantees: at-least-once vs. exactly-once, and how read receipts/delivery status are tracked
Discusses fan-out strategy for group chats as group size grows
Covers offline delivery: message queuing for disconnected users and push notification integration

text: Design a social media news feed system like Twitter/X or Instagram's home feed.
ideal_answer_points: Compares fan-out-on-write (precompute feeds when a post is made) vs. fan-out-on-read (compute feed at request time) and discusses when each wins
Addresses the 'celebrity problem' — fan-out-on-write breaking down for accounts with millions of followers, and a hybrid approach
Designs ranking/relevance beyond pure chronological order, at a high level
Discusses caching strategy for hot feeds and pagination for infinite scroll
Addresses data storage choice and justifies it against the read/write pattern

text: Design a backend system that serves an LLM-powered chatbot to millions of users, handling both latency and cost constraints.
ideal_answer_points: Addresses request queuing and batching strategy for GPU inference efficiency without unacceptable latency
Discusses streaming responses (token-by-token) to the client rather than waiting for full generation
Considers caching strategies for repeated or similar queries, including semantic/embedding-based cache lookups
Addresses cost/latency tradeoffs between model size tiers and when to route a query to a smaller vs. larger model
Discusses rate limiting, abuse prevention, and graceful degradation under load

text: Design a file storage and sharing service like Dropbox or Google Drive.
ideal_answer_points: Separates metadata storage (file names, folder structure, permissions) from actual file/blob storage
Discusses chunking large files for upload/download efficiency and resumable transfers
Addresses synchronization: how clients detect changes and reconcile conflicts across devices
Covers deduplication strategy (content hashing to avoid storing identical files twice)
Discusses versioning and how storage cost is managed as file history grows

text: Design a search-as-you-type autocomplete system like a search engine's query suggestions.
ideal_answer_points: Proposes a trie (prefix tree) as the core data structure for efficient prefix lookups
Discusses how to rank suggestions (frequency-based, personalization, recency) rather than just returning all matches
Addresses how the trie is kept up to date as new queries come in, without blocking read traffic
Covers latency requirements given this is on the critical typing path, and how caching top queries helps
Discusses sharding the trie/index if the dataset grows too large for a single machine

text: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube, focusing on upload processing and playback delivery.
ideal_answer_points: Discusses transcoding uploaded video into multiple resolutions/bitrates for adaptive streaming
Explains adaptive bitrate streaming (e.g., HLS/DASH) and why it matters for varying network conditions
Addresses CDN usage for serving video close to users and reducing origin server load
Covers metadata storage (video info, view counts) separately from the actual video files in object storage
Discusses handling of upload processing asynchronously via a job queue rather than blocking the upload request

text: Design a notification system that can send push, email, and SMS notifications at scale.
ideal_answer_points: Proposes a message queue-based architecture decoupling notification triggers from delivery
Discusses per-channel worker services (push/email/SMS) consuming from the queue independently
Addresses user preference management (opt-in/opt-out per channel) and how it's enforced before sending
Covers retry logic and dead-letter handling for failed deliveries
Discusses rate limiting per user to avoid notification spam and deduplication of near-simultaneous triggers

text: Design a distributed caching system like Redis, covering how it scales across multiple machines.
ideal_answer_points: Discusses consistent hashing for distributing keys across cache nodes and minimizing reshuffling when nodes are added/removed
Addresses cache eviction policies (LRU, LFU) and when each is appropriate
Covers replication strategy for fault tolerance and read scaling
Discusses cache invalidation strategies and the tradeoffs between TTL-based and explicit invalidation
Addresses the thundering herd problem when a hot key expires and how to mitigate it

text: Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult project.
ideal_answer_points: Uses STAR structure: sets clear situation/task context before describing actions
Focuses on their own individual actions and decisions, not just what 'the team' did
Describes concrete steps taken to lead — delegation, unblocking others, communication cadence
Ends with a specific, ideally quantifiable result
Reflects on what they'd do differently, showing self-awareness rather than a purely self-congratulatory story

text: Describe a time you disagreed with a manager or teammate. How did you handle it?
ideal_answer_points: Describes the disagreement factually and respectfully, without disparaging the other person
Explains their reasoning for their position and how they made their case
Shows they listened to the other perspective, not just pushed their own view
Describes the resolution and their own role in reaching it
Reflects on the outcome and what it taught them about handling disagreement professionally

text: Tell me about a time you had to solve a problem with limited resources or information.
ideal_answer_points: Clearly describes the constraint (time, budget, information, tooling) that made the problem hard
Explains the approach taken to work within or around the constraint
Shows resourcefulness and independent judgment rather than waiting for someone else to solve it
Describes the concrete outcome
Connects the experience to a broader lesson about working under constraints

text: Describe a mistake you made at work and how you handled it.
ideal_answer_points: Takes clear ownership of the mistake without deflecting blame
Describes concrete corrective action taken once the mistake was identified
Explains what changed afterward (process, habit, checklist) to prevent recurrence
Avoids picking a mistake that's either trivial or reflects poorly on core job competence
Shows genuine self-awareness and growth, not a rehearsed-sounding 'perfectionism' answer

text: Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight or seemingly impossible deadline.
ideal_answer_points: Describes how they assessed and prioritized what was actually essential under time pressure
Explains specific tradeoffs made (scope cut, help requested, process changed) and the reasoning behind them
Shows clear communication with stakeholders about risk or status during the crunch
States the outcome concretely, including whether the deadline was actually met
Reflects on what they'd change about their planning to avoid similar crunches

text: Describe a time you had to work closely with a colleague you found difficult.
ideal_answer_points: Describes the difficulty specifically and professionally, avoiding personal attacks or vague complaints
Focuses on their own adaptive behavior — how they adjusted their communication or approach
Shows empathy or attempt to understand the other person's perspective/constraints
Describes a concrete resolution or working arrangement that improved the collaboration
Avoids framing the story as 'I was right and they were wrong' without nuance

text: Tell me about a time you had to make progress on something with unclear or ambiguous requirements.
ideal_answer_points: Describes how they sought clarity (asking questions, making reasonable assumptions) rather than freezing
Explains how they decided what to build/do despite the ambiguity, and how they validated the direction
Shows comfort with iterating and adjusting course as more information became available
States a concrete outcome, including how the ambiguity was ultimately resolved
Reflects on how they'd approach similar ambiguity differently in hindsight

text: Describe a time you had to juggle multiple competing priorities. How did you decide what to focus on?
ideal_answer_points: Describes the specific competing demands clearly, not just 'I was busy'
Explains the criteria used to prioritize (impact, urgency, stakeholder needs) rather than an arbitrary choice
Shows how they communicated tradeoffs to affected stakeholders rather than silently dropping work
States the concrete outcome of the prioritization decision
Reflects on whether the prioritization held up in hindsight

text: Describe a time you received critical feedback you initially disagreed with. What did you do?
ideal_answer_points: Describes the feedback and their initial reaction honestly, without downplaying the disagreement
Shows they took time to genuinely consider the feedback rather than dismissing it outright
Explains what they did next — sought more context, tested the feedback, adjusted behavior
States the eventual outcome, including whether their view changed and why
Demonstrates emotional maturity rather than defensiveness in how the story is told

text: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond what was expected of you.
ideal_answer_points: Describes a genuinely specific instance, not a vague generalization about work ethic
Clarifies what the baseline expectation was, so the 'above and beyond' part is clear by contrast
Explains the motivation — why they chose to go further, not just that they did
States a concrete, ideally measurable impact of the extra effort
Avoids sounding self-congratulatory; frames it as judgment and initiative, not just extra hours
